meta.blurb: On her last day as a counselor, Marianne Cole hears one client finally speak about the night his sister died. Then he hands her a key and vanishes. Bound by her promise to keep secrets, she must decide how far to go to save him.
meta.bible: Marianne Cole: a counselor of sixty-two, calm, patient and observant, closing her practice after thirty years in Saltmere; the viewpoint of the story. Daniel Reeve: a clockmaker of thirty-four, a quiet man who has said almost nothing about his sister's death in eight months of sessions. Anna Reeve: Daniel's sister, a bookkeeper, who died in Saltmere harbour three years ago, aged twenty-seven; the police called it an accident. Owen Marsh: Daniel's friend and partner in Marsh and Reeve Clocks, warm and helpful; he is the culprit. Inspector Nora Pell: the careful local detective. Gareth Pike: the bad-tempered harbour master, who hides a small crime of his own. Mrs Dunn: Anna's old landlady, kind and sharp-eyed. Tilly Ames: Marianne's young receptionist. Saltmere: a small harbour town on the coast. Quay Street: where Marianne's office is, above the bakery. The Harbour Clock Tower: a stone tower above the quay, whose clock Daniel repairs; the clock room is at the top of a winding stair. Marsh and Reeve Clocks: the clock shop on Fisher Row. The brass key: Daniel's key to locker fourteen at the railway station, which holds Anna's ledger and diary. Facts: Anna died at quarter past nine on a night in October; her red scarf was never found, and Daniel told no one about it except Marianne, in his third session; Owen stole and sold old watches through the shop, and Anna found out. Voice and tone: calm, tense and humane, a psychological mystery told through listening; death is stated plainly with no gore; no one is hurt in the tower.

B1B2: After thirty years of listening to other people, Marianne Cole is closing her small office above the bakery. It is her last day, and she has one more client to see.
Tilly, the young receptionist, gives Marianne a hug and goes home early. Marianne is left alone to wait for her last client, Daniel Reeve, who is due at four.
Marianne opens Daniel's thin folder and remembers why he came. His sister Anna died in the harbour three years ago, and the police said that it was an accident.
Daniel Reeve arrives at four, as he always does. He is a clockmaker, thin and quiet, and he puts a small silver watch on the table between them before he speaks.
After a long silence Daniel looks straight at Marianne for the first time. He says that his sister did not fall into the harbour, and that he has always known it.
Daniel explains that Anna phoned him that night, and that she sounded afraid. By the time he reached the harbour, she was already in the water, and the watch had stopped.
Daniel says he knows who is to blame, and tonight he is going to meet that person. He gives Marianne a brass key and asks her to give it to Inspector Pell if he does not come back.
Daniel leaves the office and walks away down the street. Marianne stands at the window and wonders whether she should keep her promise to protect his secrets, or break it to protect his life.
Marianne phones Daniel again and again, but he does not answer. At six o'clock she decides that she cannot wait any longer, and she calls Inspector Nora Pell.
Inspector Pell and Marianne go to Marsh and Reeve Clocks on Fisher Row. The door is open, a cup of tea stands cold on the bench, and every clock in the shop has stopped at quarter past nine.
Owen Marsh, Daniel's friend and partner in the shop, hurries in looking worried. He says that Daniel has been very low lately, and he offers to help in any way he can.
That night, at home, Marianne reads her notes from Daniel's third session. He had said that Anna's red scarf was never found, and that he had told no one, not even Owen.
On Saturday morning Marianne gives the brass key to Inspector Pell. It opens locker fourteen at the railway station, and inside they find a thick ledger and a small diary.
In the police station Pell studies the ledger, which records about thirty old watches sold with no papers. Every sale is marked with the letters D and R, which stand for Daniel Reeve.
Pell says that if Daniel signed those sales, he may be the thief, and perhaps he has run away. Marianne is shaken, because she has never thought of him that way.
Marianne visits Mrs Dunn, who once let Anna a room in her house. The old woman invites her in and says that in her last weeks Anna was pale, nervous and unable to sleep.
Mrs Dunn remembers that Anna said she must speak to someone before that Friday. After her death, the old woman adds, Owen Marsh brought flowers, which she thought kind.
Gareth Pike, the harbour master, sees Marianne asking questions on the quay. He shouts that the harbour is his business, and that nobody should ask about Anna Reeve.
Pike calms down and admits that on that night three years ago he was selling fuel illegally on the quay. He says he saw Anna talking with a man in a long coat, but he could not see his face.
Late in the afternoon Owen Marsh knocks at Marianne's half-empty office with two cups of coffee. He says that he is too worried about Daniel to sit at home alone.
Owen talks sadly about Anna and says that he still has bad dreams. In them, he says, he sees her red scarf lying on the harbour steps.
Marianne hides her shock, because the scarf was never found and Daniel told no one about it, not even Owen. Only a person who had been there that night could have seen it on the steps.
Owen asks gently whether Daniel ever said anything about him. Marianne answers that she cannot discuss what clients say, and Owen smiles and says that of course he understands.
When Owen has gone, Marianne looks out of her window at the Harbour Clock Tower. Its clock is stopped at quarter past nine, though it is almost evening, and she knows that Daniel mends that clock.
Marianne understands that Daniel stopped the tower clock as a message, because he meant to meet the culprit there. She tries to call Pell, but the inspector's phone goes to voicemail.
Marianne decides that she cannot wait for the police any longer. She walks along the harbour wall in the dusk, with the wind off the sea blowing cold in her face.
At the foot of the tower Marianne finds that the small wooden door is not locked. She steps inside, switches on her phone as a torch, and begins to climb the winding stairs.
At the top of the stairs is the clock room, a high cold chamber full of great iron wheels. The machine is silent, and the only light comes from the clock face.
It is Daniel, tied to the chair with a thick cord, pale and weak but alive and awake. He looks up at her and whispers her name.
Daniel whispers that Owen came to the shop on Friday night and gave him tea. It must have held something to make him sleep, and he woke up here, tied to the chair.
Marianne begins to untie the knot, but it is tight and her fingers are cold. Then she hears slow footsteps climbing the stairs, and a light shines on the wall.
Owen Marsh appears in the doorway with a torch in his hand. He is no longer smiling, and he stands in the way of the only stairs down.
Owen says in a calm voice that Marianne is too clever and that she listened too well. He says he should never have gone to her office, and he looks tired and sad.
Marianne stands slowly and speaks in the calm, steady voice she has used for thirty years. She asks Owen how he feels, and she tells him that there is time to talk.
Owen sits down on a step and begins to talk. The shop was losing money, he says, so he sold old watches without papers, and he put Daniel's initials on the sales to cover himself.
Owen says that he met Anna at the harbour steps that night just to talk. She turned to leave, her foot slipped, and she fell into the black water before he could catch her.
Owen admits that he was afraid and ran away. He did not call for help, and he left Anna's red scarf lying on the wet steps, which he has seen every night since.
Marianne tells Owen gently that he has carried this heavy secret for three years. She says that it is not too late to put it down and tell the truth.
Owen shakes his head and says that if he lets them go, he will lose everything he has. Marianne answers quietly that he has already lost it, and that only the truth is left.
Suddenly they hear voices and many boots on the stone stairs below. A woman's voice, which Marianne knows at once, calls her name and asks if she is safe.
Owen looks at the door and at Marianne, and something in him gives way. He puts the torch down on the floor and sits beside it with his hands in the air.
Inspector Pell arrests Owen Marsh and leads him away down the stairs. A young officer cuts the cord around Daniel's hands, and he stands up slowly.
Daniel turns to Marianne with tears in his eyes and says quietly that she came after all. She answers that of course she did, because that is what a friend does.
Before they go down, Daniel steps to the great machine and moves a lever. The wheels begin to turn, the pendulum swings, and the clock strikes, for the first time in three years.
At the police station Pell tells Marianne that she was right to speak up when a life was at risk. Owen has admitted that he wrote the initials D and R in the ledger himself.
On Sunday morning Daniel comes to the empty office, where only two chairs remain. He asks if they can have one last session, and Marianne smiles and says that she has been waiting for it.
For an hour Daniel speaks about Anna, her laugh, her habits and her courage. Marianne listens without interrupting, and when he has finished, she gives the brass key back to him.
When Daniel has gone, Marianne locks her office door for the last time and posts the key through the letterbox of the bakery. Then she walks out into the cool, bright afternoon, feeling free.
Marianne walks slowly to the harbour as the sun begins to set. Above her the tower clock strikes the right hour, and she stops to listen to its slow, true voice.
Marianne thinks that her work as a counselor is over, but her listening is not. There will always be someone with a story that needs a quiet place and a patient ear.
C1C2: On the last Friday of her working life, Marianne Cole stood in a small office above the bakery in Quay Street and wrapped thirty years of books in old newspaper. The room smelled of tea, of old paper and of the warm bread that rose through the floorboards every afternoon. It seemed impossible that so many hours of other people's sorrow could be packed into a handful of cardboard boxes.

Tilly Ames, the young receptionist, hugged her employer tightly, wiped her eyes on her sleeve, and hurried home before she could say anything sentimental. Marianne remained alone to wait for her final client of all, Daniel Reeve, who was due at four and who had never been late in eight months. She thought of him with a mixture of affection and professional frustration, and she hoped, a little guiltily, that today he might finally speak.

She opened Daniel's folder, which was far thinner than any other on her shelf, and reminded herself of the little she knew. His younger sister Anna had drowned in Saltmere harbour three years earlier, and although the police had called it an accident, Daniel had never spoken of the night in all their sessions together. He sat, he drank his tea, and he left, and she had learned to be patient.

Daniel Reeve arrived at four precisely, as he always did, a thin and quiet clockmaker with ink-stained fingers and eyes that seldom stayed long on any face. Without a word of greeting he drew a small silver watch from his pocket and laid it carefully on the table between them, as another man might have laid down a letter. It had stopped, she noticed with a slight shiver, at exactly a quarter past nine, and he did not seem to want to explain why.

For a long time he sat without speaking, and Marianne, who had learned that silence is sometimes the kindest question, did not break it. Then Daniel raised his eyes to hers, quite steady, and said in a flat quiet voice that his sister had not fallen, and that he had known it from the first morning. It was the longest sentence he had spoken in her office, and it fell between them like a dropped stone.

Anna had telephoned him at nine that night, Daniel said slowly, sounding afraid, and she had said she needed to talk to someone about something she had found at work. By the time he ran down to the harbour, a quarter of an hour later, the quay was empty, and he found only the broken surface of the dark water. Her watch, which the police returned to him, had stopped at quarter past nine.

Daniel rose, and with a steadiness that frightened her, told Marianne that he now knew who was responsible and that he intended to meet that person that very night. He pressed a small brass key into her palm and asked her, if he did not come back, to give it to Inspector Nora Pell and to no one else. When she asked him who, he shook his head and said that he would not put another person in danger.

Daniel left without waiting for her answer, and Marianne watched from the window as his thin figure vanished down the street into the thickening dusk. Her profession demanded that she keep every word he had said to herself, but there were limits to that vow, and she knew that a life in danger was the clearest of them. For the first time in thirty years she felt the old rules pulling in two directions at once.

Marianne rang Daniel's number four times between five and six, and each time the telephone rang and rang until a flat electronic voice invited her to leave a message. At six o'clock she put down the receiver and decided that her duty to protect a life outweighed her duty to guard a secret, and she dialled the number of Inspector Nora Pell. She said only that she was worried about a man called Daniel Reeve, and that she thought he might be in danger.

Inspector Pell, a brisk woman in a grey raincoat, met Marianne at the clock shop on Fisher Row, where they found the door swinging open and the lights burning. A cup of tea stood cold upon the workbench, and all around them the clocks, big and small, hung silent, every one of them stopped at exactly quarter past nine. The shop felt like a room in which time itself had been told to wait.

A broad, friendly man in a good coat hurried into the shop and introduced himself as Owen Marsh, Daniel's friend and partner in the business, who had seen the lights on from the street. He seemed deeply troubled by the news, remarked that Daniel had been terribly low for weeks, and offered to help the police in any way he could. Marianne noticed, with a small and unwelcome prickle of suspicion, that the offer of help came very quickly indeed.

Late that night, in her quiet kitchen, Marianne spread the notes of her eight months with Daniel across the table and read them again by the light of a lamp. In the record of the third session she found a single odd remark, that Anna's red scarf had never been found and that Daniel had told no one about it, not the police and not even Owen. It was a tiny, forgotten detail, and she copied it out carefully on a clean sheet of paper.

On Saturday morning Marianne handed Daniel's brass key to Inspector Pell, as she had promised, and together they walked to the railway station and found the row of old iron lockers. Locker fourteen swung open at the first turn of the key, and inside lay two items wrapped in a plain cloth, a thick account ledger and a small leather diary. Pell lifted them out as carefully as if they had been made of glass.

At the police station, Pell turned the pages of the ledger with a growing frown, and it soon became clear what they had found. About thirty antique watches had been sold through Marsh and Reeve Clocks without proper papers, and each sale carried the same pair of initials, D and R, which stood for Daniel Reeve. In the diary, Anna's neat handwriting spoke of fear and secrecy, though it named no name.

Inspector Pell leaned back in her chair and observed, not unkindly, that a man whose initials were on every sale might be a thief, and that a thief who disappears has often simply run away. Marianne was shaken, for in eight months she had seen nothing in Daniel Reeve but grief, and she was forced to ask herself whether she had been deceived. Doubt, she reflected, was the most uncomfortable thing a counselor could ever feel, since people came to her precisely because she did not have any.

Mrs Dunn, who had once let a room to Anna Reeve, opened her red front door and led Marianne into a small parlour full of china dogs. She remembered Anna's last weeks with perfect clarity, she said: the girl had grown pale and nervous, had stopped eating properly, and had been out of the house at all hours. Something at the shop had been troubling her, though she never said what it was, and Mrs Dunn had never dared to ask her directly.

Anna had once muttered, Mrs Dunn recalled, that she must speak to someone before that Friday, and that she could not carry the secret a day longer. After the girl died, that lovely Mr Marsh had called with a bunch of white roses, and the old lady had been very touched by his kindness. Marianne thanked her, and said nothing at all about the small cold feeling that had settled in her chest.

On the quay, a large man in a heavy coat marched up to Marianne and demanded to know why a stranger was asking questions about Anna Reeve. It was Gareth Pike, the harbour master, a notoriously ill-tempered man whose red face grew redder as he insisted that the harbour was his business and that the matter had been closed for three years. His anger, Marianne thought, was suspiciously loud, the anger of a man who was far more frightened than he wished anyone to see.

When Marianne asked him quietly why he was so afraid, Pike's anger drained away, and he muttered that on the night in question he had been selling fuel from the quay without a licence. He had not dared to tell the police what he had seen, he admitted, which was Anna Reeve arguing at the fish steps with a tall man in a long coat and a grey cap. He had never seen the man's face, he insisted, and had spent three uneasy years wondering whether he should have spoken up sooner.

Late on Saturday afternoon, Owen Marsh knocked on the door of Marianne's half-emptied office, carrying two cups of coffee and wearing a look of kindly concern. He could not bear to sit at home alone, he said, and he hoped she did not mind if he sat with her for a few minutes among the boxes. Marianne, who had no good reason to refuse and every reason to listen, invited him in and cleared a space for him on the old sofa.

Owen talked for a long time about Anna and about how deeply her death had marked them all, and then his voice dropped. He still had terrible dreams, he told Marianne, in which he saw Anna's red scarf lying on the harbour steps, as bright as a flag against the wet stone. He rubbed his eyes with the back of his hand and looked at her with great sorrow.

Marianne held her cup quite still and kept her face carefully calm, though her mind raced. Anna's scarf had never been found, and Daniel had sworn to her in confidence that he had told nobody about it, not the police and not even his partner. Only someone who had stood on those wet steps on the night of Anna's death could have seen it lying there, and Owen Marsh was telling her so himself.

Owen leaned forward and asked, in the lightest of tones, whether Daniel had ever mentioned him in their sessions. Marianne replied that she was not free to discuss anything a client had told her, and he smiled warmly and said of course, of course, he quite understood, and finished his coffee. Only when he stood to leave did she notice that his hands had begun to tremble.

When Owen had gone, Marianne walked to the window to clear her head and found her gaze resting on the Harbour Clock Tower at the end of the quay. Its great white face had stopped at quarter past nine, though it was nearly evening, and she remembered that Daniel Reeve kept that clock in order. A cold thought came to her, that every clock he touched had been set to the same hour.

Suddenly it all fell into place, and Marianne understood that Daniel had stopped the tower clock as a signal and had planned to meet the guilty person at the very place where time had stopped for his sister. She called Inspector Pell at once, but the telephone rang to the end and gave her a recorded voice, so she left a message that was brief and urgent. Then, against all her better judgment and every rule that she had ever taught a client, she picked up her coat and went out into the dusk.

Marianne decided that she could not wait for the inspector, since a man who had been missing for a day and a half might not have many hours left. She walked rapidly along the harbour wall in the failing light, her collar turned up against the cold wind from the sea. Never in thirty years had she done anything so rash, and never had she felt so sure.

At the foot of the stone tower stood a low wooden door, and to her surprise it yielded to her push and opened with a long, soft creak. Marianne switched on the torch of her mobile telephone and began to climb the narrow spiral stair, counting the steps under her breath to keep her courage. The air grew colder and damper with every turn, and the silence thickened around her.

At the top of the stair she emerged into the heart of the clock, a high, cold chamber crowded with great iron wheels, chains and weights that hung down into the dark. The ancient mechanism was perfectly silent, and the only light fell in pale bars through the back of the great white clock face. In the middle of the floor, among the shadows, sat a figure tied to a chair.

It was Daniel Reeve, bound to a wooden chair with a thick cord, pale and unshaven but alive, and his eyes opened wide at the sound of her footsteps. He whispered her name in a voice so dry that it seemed to come from very far away, and Marianne, forgetting every rule of her profession, dropped to her knees and took his cold hands in hers. For a long moment neither of them could find a single word to say.

Between sips from the bottle of water that Marianne held to his lips, Daniel explained in a cracked whisper that Owen had come to the shop on Friday evening and made him a cup of tea. It must have been drugged, because the next thing he remembered was waking in the clock room with his hands tied behind him, in the dark, hours later. Owen had said only that he would come back later, he added, and that nobody would think of looking for him in such a place.

Marianne began to pick at the knots with her cold fingers, but the cord was thick, and she had made little progress when a sound reached her from below. Slow, heavy footsteps were climbing the spiral stair, and a yellow light bobbed along the curving wall and grew brighter with every step. Daniel's face, in the growing beam of light, turned the colour of chalk, and he whispered to her that she should run while she still could.

Owen Marsh stepped into the clock room with a torch in one hand, and for the first time since she had met him he was not smiling. He stood in the doorway with his broad shoulders filling the opening, so that the only way out was entirely blocked, and the torchlight swung slowly across the three of them. Behind him, the stone stair dropped away into the dark like the mouth of a well, and no sound came up from the town below.

I knew you were clever, Owen said to Marianne at last, in a quiet, tired voice, and I knew when I came to your office that I should have stayed away. You listened too well, he added with a faint sad smile, and I talked too much, which is exactly what people do in that room. It was the speech of a man who had run out of ways to pretend.

Marianne rose slowly to her feet, keeping her hands visible and her voice low and even, in the manner she had practised for thirty years in her quiet room. She asked Owen how he was feeling and told him that there was no hurry, and that she would listen to whatever he wished to say. It was the oldest of her skills, and she had never needed it more.

Owen sat down heavily on the stone step and, almost as if he had been waiting for years to be asked, began to talk. The shop had been failing, he said, and so he had started selling stolen antique watches from his private collection and writing Daniel's initials against each sale in case anyone ever asked. Anna, who kept the accounts, had found out in the autumn and had refused to keep his secret.

On that October night, Owen said, he had met Anna at the foot of the fish steps simply to ask her for time, and the argument had grown loud and desperate in the dark. She had turned to walk away, he swore, and her foot had slid on the wet stone, and before he could seize her arm she was gone into the black water. He did not know, he said, whether he could any longer believe his own story, which he had told himself so many times in the dark.

He had been terrified, he confessed, and instead of shouting for help he had turned and run, leaving the girl's red scarf lying on the wet steps like a bright signal in the dark. He had never gone near the harbour at night since, he said, and yet he had seen that scarf every single night in his sleep for three years. His voice cracked, and he covered his face with his shaking hands as though to shut out the sight.

Marianne moved a step closer, and in the gentlest voice she possessed she told Owen that he had carried this burden alone for three years and that nobody could be expected to bear such a weight for ever. It was not too late to put it down, she said, and to let the truth be spoken aloud in daylight. Owen lifted his wet face, and for a moment she thought he would agree.

Then his face hardened, and Owen shook his head and said that if he let them walk down those stairs, he would lose the shop, his name and his freedom all at once. Marianne answered him very quietly that he had already lost the things that mattered most, three years ago, on the harbour steps, and that all that remained to him was the chance to be honest. The words fell into the silence like pebbles into a deep well, and Marianne waited without moving to hear whether any answer would come back.

Suddenly the silence was torn by a clatter of boots on the stairs, and the sound of several people climbing fast, and a voice that Marianne knew at once called out her name. It was Inspector Pell, who had got the message and had come with two officers, and she was shouting for Marianne to say whether she was safe. Owen froze where he sat, and the torch trembled in his hand so that the shadows leapt about the walls.

Owen looked at the door, then at Marianne, and something seemed to give way in his face, as though a long-held breath had at last been released. He laid the torch carefully on the stone floor, sat down beside it, and lifted his empty hands to show that he would not fight. When Inspector Pell burst in with her officers at her back, there was nothing left for her to prevent and nothing at all for her to fear.

Inspector Pell arrested Owen Marsh in a few quiet sentences and handed him to two officers, who led him slowly down the winding stair. Another officer cut the cord from Daniel's wrists, and the clockmaker rose on stiff and trembling legs and stood rubbing his hands as the colour crept back into his face. Pell gave Marianne a long, level look that held both a mild reproach and a good deal of unspoken admiration, and said that they would talk in the morning.

Daniel turned to Marianne with tears standing in his tired eyes and said, very quietly, that she had come after all. Of course she had come, Marianne answered, for that was precisely what a friend did, and she had never in thirty years used the word about a client before. He took her hand in both of his, and neither of them noticed the officers politely looking away.

Before they left the tower, Daniel limped over to the great machine and, with the sure touch of a craftsman, set the heavy pendulum swinging once more. The wheels began to turn, the iron teeth caught, and the clock face moved slowly forward from quarter past nine, and a moment later the great bell above them struck the hour over the dark harbour. It was the first time in three years that the tower had told the true time.

At the police station, over a cup of strong tea, Inspector Pell assured Marianne that the law and her own profession agreed that a person in danger must be protected, and that she had been right to break her silence. Owen had confessed that he had written the initials D and R against every sale in Anna's ledger himself, which cleared Daniel completely. She added, with a dry smile, that she would not recommend the tower to anyone over sixty.

On Sunday morning, Daniel Reeve climbed the stairs above the bakery to find Marianne's office stripped bare except for two chairs and a low table by the window. He asked whether they might have one last session, a proper one, and Marianne, who had thought her working life was over, smiled and said that she had been waiting eight months to hear that question. They sat down opposite each other in the sunshine, and the old room seemed to settle around them as it had done a thousand times before.

For a whole hour Daniel talked about his sister, her laugh, her stubbornness, the songs she sang badly and the courage that had led her to confront a friend, and Marianne listened without speaking or taking a single note. When at last he fell quiet, she took the brass key from her pocket and placed it in his hand, because the locker was empty now and its secret finally told. He wept then, freely and for a long time, as he had never done in front of anyone, and Marianne let the silence do its patient work.

When Daniel had gone, Marianne carried her last box down to the street, locked the door of the office for the final time, and dropped the key through the letterbox of the bakery below. The afternoon was cool and bright, and the smell of fresh bread followed her out into Quay Street like a blessing. She felt lighter than she had in thirty years, and strangely unafraid of the long empty days ahead.

Marianne walked slowly down to the harbour as the sun went down, and above the roofs of Saltmere the tower clock began to strike, slow and clear and perfectly correct. She stopped at the end of the quay and listened to every note, thinking of a thin man in an empty room, and of a girl whose last Friday had finally been understood. The water below her shone like polished copper in the last of the sun, and for once even the gulls were quiet, as if they too were listening.

Standing at the end of the quay as the last light faded, Marianne understood that her years as a counselor had ended, but that the listening at their heart would never end, for it was simply another word for kindness. There would always be somebody in the world carrying a story too heavy to hold alone, and somewhere a quiet room with an open door and a patient ear. She turned and walked home through the lamplit streets, and behind her the clock struck again.
